stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
After engineers filled a new reservoir in 2019, seismometers in the surrounding valley recorded three times as many small earthquakes as in the previous year. Geologist Mara Lindqvist concluded that the weight of the stored water had triggered the additional tremors.

Text 2
The increase in recorded tremors near the reservoir is real. However, a denser network of seismometers was installed in the valley that same year, and it could simply be detecting small earthquakes that the older, sparser network had missed.
choices: The weight of the reservoir's water caused the valley's additional earthquakes.
More small earthquakes were recorded in the valley after the reservoir was filled.
The new seismometer network fully accounts for the rise in recorded earthquakes.
The reported rise in the valley's earthquakes came from a measurement error.
explanation: This is groundwork for 'same evidence, different cause' questions. Split Text 1 into its observation (more tremors were recorded) and its inference (the water's weight caused them). Text 2 opens by accepting the observation ('The increase... is real') and attacks only the inference. So the one thing both authors accept is the observation itself.

A.why: You picked Text 1's conclusion. Text 2 offers a different explanation for the rise, so it doesn't accept this cause. That puts it on one side only.

C.why: You picked Text 2's alternative and made it stronger. Text 2 only says the network 'could' explain the rise, and Text 1 credits the water, so neither author would sign this.

D.why: This is the trap. Text 2 doesn't say the data are wrong. It calls the increase 'real' and questions only what caused it to be recorded.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
In the year after Ridgeport raised its minimum wage, the number of teenagers employed at the city's fast-food restaurants fell by 8 percent. Economist Dana Ofori therefore argues that the higher wage led restaurant owners to hire fewer teenage workers.

Text 2
Although teenage employment at Ridgeport's fast-food restaurants did decline, a large warehouse opened outside the city that year offering higher hourly pay. The drop could reflect teenagers leaving restaurant jobs for the warehouse rather than owners cutting positions.
choices: Ridgeport's restaurant owners cut teenage jobs in response to the new wage.
The warehouse drew teenagers away from Ridgeport's fast-food restaurants.
Teenage employment at Ridgeport's fast-food restaurants never actually declined.
Fewer teenagers worked at Ridgeport's fast-food restaurants after the wage rose.
explanation: This builds the first step of 'same evidence, different cause' questions: telling what was observed apart from what was inferred. Text 1 observes an 8 percent drop and infers that the wage caused it. Text 2's concession ('Although... did decline') accepts the drop and offers the warehouse as another cause. The drop is the shared ground.

A.why: You picked Text 1's inference. Text 2 suggests the drop came from teenagers leaving 'rather than owners cutting positions,' so it doesn't accept this.

B.why: You picked Text 2's rival cause and stated it as fact. Text 2 says only that the drop 'could' reflect this, and Text 1 never mentions the warehouse.

C.why: This is the trap. Text 2 doesn't deny the decline. It says the decline happened and questions only why.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
This season, sprinters at Halvorsen University who switched to carbon-plated spikes lowered their 100-meter times by an average of 0.15 seconds. Coach Teo Barrera concluded that the new spikes made his athletes faster.

Text 2
Certainly the Halvorsen sprinters ran faster times this season. But most of their races took place on the university's newly resurfaced track, and a firmer surface alone could have produced an improvement of that size, with or without new spikes.
choices: Halvorsen's sprinters who switched spikes recorded faster times this season.
The carbon-plated spikes were what made Halvorsen's sprinters faster.
The resurfaced track was the true source of the sprinters' faster times.
The sprinters' improved times this season were likely recorded incorrectly.
explanation: This is groundwork for 'same evidence, different cause' questions. Text 1's observation is the faster times, and its inference is that the spikes caused them. Text 2's 'Certainly... But' structure grants the observation and then proposes the new track surface as another cause. Both authors accept that the times improved.

B.why: You picked Text 1's conclusion. Text 2 argues the track could explain the gain 'with or without new spikes,' so it doesn't accept this.

C.why: You turned Text 2's possibility into a certainty. Text 2 says the surface 'could have' done it, and Text 1 credits the spikes.

D.why: This is the trap. Text 2 opens by saying the sprinters 'ran faster times.' It accepts the measurement and disputes only the cause.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
In the year after the city of Brennick added protected bike lanes to Elm Avenue, traffic injuries on that street fell by one third. City planners concluded that the protected lanes had made Elm Avenue safer.

Text 2
While injuries on Elm Avenue clearly dropped after the bike lanes opened, the city also lowered the street's speed limit that same month. It is difficult to exclude the possibility that slower driving, not the lanes, produced the decline.
choices: The protected bike lanes were responsible for Elm Avenue's fewer injuries.
The lower speed limit was responsible for Elm Avenue's fewer injuries.
Traffic injuries on Elm Avenue fell after the protected bike lanes were added.
Traffic injuries on Elm Avenue did not truly fall after the lanes were added.
explanation: This builds the skill behind 'same evidence, different cause' questions. Text 1's observation is that injuries fell by a third, and its inference is that the lanes caused the drop. Text 2's 'While... clearly dropped' grants the observation, and 'difficult to exclude' introduces the speed limit as a rival cause. The drop in injuries is what both accept.

A.why: You picked Text 1's inference. Text 2 raises the possibility that slower driving, 'not the lanes,' produced the decline, so it doesn't accept this.

B.why: You stated Text 2's alternative as settled. Text 2 says only that it can't be excluded, and Text 1 never mentions the speed limit.

D.why: This is the trap. Text 2 says injuries 'clearly dropped.' It challenges the explanation, not the observation.
